> **Note:** The data, model and results in this document are simulated and hypothetical. They demonstrate how the evaluation and reporting would work, not real farm results.

# 1. Introduction and Objective

Building a predictive model is only half the job. A model is useful to an agribusiness only if its accuracy is measured honestly, its weaknesses are understood, and its results are explained in a way that farm managers, procurement teams and executives can act on.

**Hypothetical model.** The strategy is built around a regression model that predicts crop yield (tonnes per hectare, t/ha) for each farm plot before harvest, using rainfall, temperature, fertilizer use, soil quality and region. Yield forecasts feed procurement, storage, logistics and pricing decisions, so forecast errors have a direct cost.

The objectives of the evaluation are to:

- measure how close predictions are to real outcomes using standard metrics;
- check that the model is reliable across regions and seasons, not just on average;
- present results visually so non-technical stakeholders can understand them;
- summarize performance and recommendations in an executive summary; and
- state limitations openly and plan further refinement.

# 2. Evaluation Design

## 2.1 Simulated data

Because this is a strategy document, a synthetic dataset of farm plots is generated. The West region is deliberately made noisier so the evaluation has a realistic weak spot to find.

```{r data}
set.seed(123)
n <- 700

farms <- data.frame(
  year         = sample(2018:2024, n, replace = TRUE),
  region       = sample(c("North", "South", "East", "West", "Central"), n, replace = TRUE),
  rainfall     = rnorm(n, 800, 150),
  temperature  = rnorm(n, 27, 2.5),
  fertilizer   = runif(n, 60, 160),
  soil_quality = runif(n, 3, 9)
)

region_noise <- c(North = 0.25, South = 0.35, East = 0.30, West = 0.55, Central = 0.28)

farms$yield <- 0.8 +
  0.0025 * farms$rainfall -
  0.04   * (farms$temperature - 27)^2 +
  0.012  * farms$fertilizer +
  0.18   * farms$soil_quality +
  rnorm(n, 0, region_noise[farms$region])

farms$region <- factor(farms$region)
head(farms) %>% kable(digits = 2)
```

## 2.2 Data splitting

Crop data is time-ordered, so the split follows time rather than being random. This mimics real use, where the model forecasts a future season from past ones, and prevents information from the future leaking into training.

- **Training set:** seasons 2018 to 2021
- **Validation set:** season 2022 (for tuning and comparing candidates)
- **Test set:** seasons 2023 and 2024 (touched only once, for final reporting)

```{r split}
train <- farms %>% filter(year <= 2021)
valid <- farms %>% filter(year == 2022)
test  <- farms %>% filter(year >= 2023)

data.frame(Set = c("Training", "Validation", "Test"),
           Seasons = c("2018-2021", "2022", "2023-2024"),
           Plots = c(nrow(train), nrow(valid), nrow(test))) %>% kable()
```

## 2.3 Model and baseline

Every model is compared with a simple baseline so stakeholders can see the value it adds. The baseline predicts each region's long-term average yield from the training data.

```{r models}
model <- lm(yield ~ rainfall + temperature + I((temperature - 27)^2) +
              fertilizer + soil_quality + region, data = train)

baseline_means <- train %>% group_by(region) %>% summarise(base_pred = mean(yield))

test <- left_join(test, baseline_means, by = "region")
test$pred      <- as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = test))
test$error     <- test$yield - test$pred
test$abs_error <- abs(test$error)
```

# 3. Performance Metrics

## 3.1 Metric definitions

| Metric | Formula | Plain-language meaning |
|:--|:--|:--|
| MAE | mean of \|actual - predicted\| | Typical forecast miss, in t/ha |
| RMSE | square root of mean of (actual - predicted)^2 | Like MAE but penalizes large misses more |
| R-squared | 1 - SSE / SST | Share of yield variation explained by the model |
| MAPE | mean of \|error\| / actual, in % | Average error as a percentage |
| Bias | mean of (predicted - actual) | Systematic over- or under-prediction |

## 3.2 Metric functions

```{r metric-functions}
mae  <- function(a, p) mean(abs(a - p))
rmse <- function(a, p) sqrt(mean((a - p)^2))
r2   <- function(a, p) 1 - sum((a - p)^2) / sum((a - mean(a))^2)
mape <- function(a, p) mean(abs(a - p) / a) * 100
bias <- function(a, p) mean(p - a)

evaluate <- function(a, p) {
  c(MAE = mae(a, p), RMSE = rmse(a, p), R2 = r2(a, p),
    MAPE_pct = mape(a, p), Bias = bias(a, p))
}
```

## 3.3 Worked example

Five plots are used to show how the numbers are calculated.

```{r worked-example}
ex <- data.frame(Plot = LETTERS[1:5],
                 Actual = c(3.2, 4.1, 2.8, 3.9, 3.5),
                 Predicted = c(3.0, 4.4, 2.6, 3.7, 3.9))
ex$Error <- ex$Actual - ex$Predicted
ex$Squared_Error <- ex$Error^2
kable(ex, digits = 2)

round(evaluate(ex$Actual, ex$Predicted), 2)
```

## 3.4 Results on the test set

```{r overall-metrics}
overall <- rbind(
  Model    = evaluate(test$yield, test$pred),
  Baseline = evaluate(test$yield, test$base_pred)
)
kable(round(overall, 3), caption = "Test-set performance: model vs baseline")

improvement <- (1 - overall["Model", "RMSE"] / overall["Baseline", "RMSE"]) * 100
```

The model reduces RMSE by about **`r round(improvement, 0)`%** compared with the regional-average baseline.

## 3.5 Success thresholds

Targets are agreed with business users before testing, so results are judged against a pre-set standard. The values below are examples.

```{r thresholds}
thresholds <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("MAE (t/ha)", "RMSE (t/ha)", "R-squared", "MAPE (%)", "Bias (t/ha)"),
  Target = c("<= 0.30", "<= 0.40", ">= 0.80", "<= 10", "within +/- 0.05"),
  Acceptable = c("0.30 - 0.45", "0.40 - 0.55", "0.65 - 0.80", "10 - 15", "within +/- 0.10"),
  Needs_Action = c("> 0.45", "> 0.55", "< 0.65", "> 15", "beyond +/- 0.10")
)
kable(thresholds)
```

## 3.6 Segment-level evaluation

An overall score can hide local problems, so metrics are also broken down by region.

```{r by-region}
by_region <- test %>%
  group_by(Region = region) %>%
  summarise(Plots = n(),
            MAE   = mean(abs_error),
            RMSE  = sqrt(mean(error^2)),
            Bias  = mean(pred - yield)) %>%
  mutate(Status = case_when(MAE <= 0.30 ~ "On target",
                            MAE <= 0.45 ~ "Watch",
                            TRUE        ~ "Action needed"))
kable(by_region, digits = 3)
```

# 4. Visualization Plan

Each chart answers one plain question and can be understood in about ten seconds.

| Chart | Question it answers | Main audience |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Predicted vs actual scatter | How close are forecasts to reality? | Everyone |
| Residual plot | Are errors random or patterned? | Analysts |
| Error by region bar chart | Where does the model work well or poorly? | Regional managers |
| Error distribution histogram | How big are typical and worst-case errors? | Risk and finance |
| Model vs baseline bars | Is the model better than the simple approach? | Executives |

## 4.1 Predicted vs actual

```{r plot-pred-actual, fig.cap="Points close to the dashed line indicate accurate forecasts."}
ggplot(test, aes(x = yield, y = pred)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2E7D32", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  labs(title = "Predicted vs Actual Yield",
       x = "Actual yield (t/ha)", y = "Predicted yield (t/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 4.2 Residual plot

```{r plot-residuals, fig.cap="Errors scattered evenly around zero suggest no systematic bias."}
ggplot(test, aes(x = pred, y = error)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#F9A825", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  labs(title = "Residual Plot",
       x = "Predicted yield (t/ha)", y = "Error (actual - predicted)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 4.3 Error by region

```{r plot-region, fig.cap="Bars are coloured by whether each region meets the 0.30 t/ha target."}
ggplot(by_region, aes(x = Region, y = MAE, fill = Status)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.30, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("On target" = "#2E7D32", "Watch" = "#F9A825",
                               "Action needed" = "#C62828")) +
  labs(title = "Average Error by Region",
       y = "Mean absolute error (t/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 4.4 Error distribution

```{r plot-hist, fig.cap="A narrow, centred shape is good; long tails mean occasional large misses."}
ggplot(test, aes(x = error)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#2E7D32", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Forecast Errors",
       x = "Error (actual - predicted, t/ha)", y = "Number of plots") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 4.5 Model vs baseline

```{r plot-baseline, fig.cap="A lower bar means smaller forecast error."}
cmp <- data.frame(Method = c("Baseline", "Model"),
                  RMSE = c(overall["Baseline", "RMSE"], overall["Model", "RMSE"]))
ggplot(cmp, aes(x = Method, y = RMSE, fill = Method)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Baseline = "grey60", Model = "#2E7D32")) +
  labs(title = "Forecast Error: Model vs Baseline", y = "RMSE (t/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 4.6 Design principles for non-expert audiences

- One message per chart, with the takeaway in the title.
- Use business units (t/ha, or rupees of impact) instead of abstract statistics.
- Use a consistent colour code: green on target, amber watch, red action needed.
- Always show a reference line (perfect prediction or target).
- Keep charts uncluttered, and use colour-blind-friendly palettes and readable fonts.
- Show uncertainty, since forecasts are estimates and not guarantees.

# 5. Reporting Strategy

## 5.1 Tailoring the report to stakeholders

| Stakeholder | What they need to know | Format | Frequency |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Executives | Is the model reliable enough for decisions? | One-page summary with 3-4 charts | Each season |
| Regional managers | How accurate is it for my region? | Dashboard with regional views | Monthly in season |
| Procurement and logistics | How much error should I plan for? | Forecast ranges and error bands | Before each buying cycle |
| Agronomists and data team | Why does the model behave this way? | Full technical report | After every retraining |

## 5.2 Structure of the full report

1. Executive summary (one page)
2. Model and data overview
3. Evaluation method: splits, validation, baselines
4. Results: headline metrics against targets
5. Segment analysis by region and season
6. Error analysis: residuals and worst cases
7. Limitations and risks
8. Recommendations and next steps
9. Appendix: detailed tables and glossary

## 5.3 Executive summary (auto-filled from the results)

```{r exec-values, include=FALSE}
m <- overall["Model", ]
worst <- by_region %>% arrange(desc(MAE)) %>% slice(1)
n_ok  <- sum(by_region$Status == "On target")
```

**Bottom line.** The model meets the 0.30 t/ha accuracy target in `r n_ok` of `r nrow(by_region)` regions and is suitable for procurement and storage planning there.

**Accuracy.** On unseen test seasons, forecasts were off by an average of `r round(m["MAE"], 2)` t/ha (MAE), about `r round(m["MAPE_pct"], 1)`% of actual yield. The model explains `r round(m["R2"] * 100, 0)`% of the variation in yield between plots (R-squared = `r round(m["R2"], 2)`).

**Value added.** Compared with the regional-average baseline, RMSE falls by about `r round(improvement, 0)`% (`r round(m["RMSE"], 2)` vs `r round(overall["Baseline", "RMSE"], 2)` t/ha).

**Watch-out.** The **`r worst$Region`** region has the largest average error (`r round(worst$MAE, 2)` t/ha).

**Recommendation.** Approve for planning use in on-target regions; treat forecasts for `r worst$Region` with caution until the model is improved with better local data.

**Next steps.** Add irrigation and satellite vegetation data, retrain before next season, and re-test with the same metrics and targets.

## 5.4 Communication guidelines

- Lead with the conclusion and the decision it supports, then give the evidence.
- Replace jargon with plain language and define technical terms once in the appendix.
- Translate errors into business impact, such as tonnes of stock over- or under-ordered.
- Be upfront about uncertainty and where the model should not be trusted.
- Use the same metrics, targets and chart styles every season.

# 6. Interpreting Results and Recommending Improvements

| What the evaluation shows | Likely cause | Recommended action |
|:--|:--|:--|
| High error on training and test data | Model too simple or inputs missing | Add features (irrigation, pests, satellite index); try a more flexible model |
| Low training error, high test error | Overfitting | Simplify, regularize, add data, use stricter cross-validation |
| RMSE much larger than MAE | A few very large errors | Investigate outliers and extreme-weather seasons |
| Consistent over- or under-prediction | Conditions shifted, or skewed data | Recalibrate and retrain on recent seasons |
| One region or crop performs poorly | Too little or different local data | Collect more local data or build a regional model |
| Curved or funnel-shaped residuals | Relationship not captured | Transform variables, add interactions, try non-linear models |

A quick check for the second row, comparing training and test error:

```{r overfit-check}
train_pred <- predict(model, newdata = train)
data.frame(Set = c("Training", "Test"),
           RMSE = c(rmse(train$yield, train_pred), rmse(test$yield, test$pred))) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

# 7. Limitations and Further Refinement

## 7.1 Potential limitations

- **Data quality and gaps:** missing, late or inaccurate records and inconsistent units.
- **Limited history:** rare events such as severe droughts or floods may be untested.
- **Changing conditions:** climate change, new varieties and practices cause concept drift.
- **Spatial and temporal correlation:** neighbouring farms and consecutive seasons are related, so random splits look too optimistic.
- **Metric limits:** R-squared can look high even when absolute errors are large; MAPE misbehaves for low yields; RMSE is sensitive to outliers.
- **Unequal cost of errors:** under- and over-forecasting rarely cost the same, yet standard metrics treat them alike.
- **Representativeness:** results may not transfer to smallholders or unseen regions.
- **Uncertainty:** a single predicted number can give a false sense of precision.

## 7.2 Suggestions for refinement

- Enrich the data with satellite imagery, soil sensors, irrigation, and pest and disease records.
- Report prediction intervals (for example 3.4 t/ha, likely between 3.0 and 3.8).
- Add a cost-weighted metric reflecting the financial cost of over- and under-forecasting.
- Compare linear models, random forests and gradient boosting, and ensemble the best.
- Build targeted models for weak regions or crops.
- Stress-test on drought, flood and heat-wave seasons.
- Use feature importance or SHAP values so agronomists can sanity-check the model.

A simple example of a prediction interval from the fitted model:

```{r interval}
pred_int <- as.data.frame(predict(model, newdata = head(test, 5),
                                  interval = "prediction", level = 0.90))
interval_table <- data.frame(Plot      = 1:5,
                             Actual    = head(test$yield, 5),
                             Predicted = pred_int$fit,
                             Lower_90  = pred_int$lwr,
                             Upper_90  = pred_int$upr)
kable(interval_table, digits = 2)
```

## 7.3 Ongoing monitoring

Forecasts are compared with actual harvest results each season, metrics are tracked on a dashboard, and alerts fire if error exceeds the agreed thresholds. The model is retrained at least once per season and re-evaluated with the same procedure so results stay comparable and drift is caught early.

# 8. Evaluation Workflow and Timeline

| Step | Activity | Output | Timing |
|:-:|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Agree metrics and thresholds with stakeholders | Signed-off target table | Before modelling |
| 2 | Prepare test data and baselines | Locked test set, baseline scores | Week 1 |
| 3 | Run validation and calculate metrics | Overall and segment metric tables | Week 2 |
| 4 | Error analysis and diagnostics | Residual plots, worst-case review | Week 2 |
| 5 | Build visuals and dashboard | Chart set and dashboard | Week 3 |
| 6 | Write executive summary and full report | Audience-specific reports | Week 3 |
| 7 | Stakeholder review and decisions | Approval and refinement plan | Week 4 |
| 8 | Monitor and re-evaluate | Seasonal re-evaluation report | Each season |

# 9. Conclusion

This strategy gives a methodical way to judge a yield forecasting model and explain the verdict clearly. A fair test design makes results trustworthy, a balanced set of metrics shows both typical and worst-case performance, consistent visuals and audience-specific reports turn numbers into decisions, and an honest account of limitations with a monitoring plan keeps the model useful as conditions change.

The key question moves from "how accurate is the model?" to "where can we rely on it, where should we be careful, and what should we improve next?"

# Appendix: Glossary

| Term | Simple explanation |
|:--|:--|
| Residual | Gap between the real value and the prediction for one plot |
| Overfitting | A model memorizes training data and does poorly on new data |
| Cross-validation | Testing on several slices of data for a more reliable score |
| Baseline | A very simple forecast used as a benchmark |
| Bias | Consistent tendency to predict too high or too low |
| Concept drift | Real-world change that makes past learning less accurate |
| Prediction interval | Range expected to contain the true value at a stated confidence |
| t/ha | Tonnes per hectare |
